topics.title: 2.1.1 The Objectives of Government Economic Policy
2.2.2 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply Analysis
2.2.4 Aggregate Demand and the Level of Economic Activity

cards.front: State the four main objectives of government macroeconomic policy in the AQA specification.
cards.back:
Economic growth; price stability (low and stable inflation — the UK's 2% CPI target); minimising unemployment; and a stable balance of payments on current account.

AQA also expects awareness of further objectives — balancing the government budget, a more equitable distribution of income, and environmental protection — and that the importance attached to each objective changes over time.

cards.front: Give the UK's usual targets for growth, unemployment and inflation, and why each matters.
cards.back:
Growth — sustainable, around 2–3%: raises incomes, living standards, employment and tax revenue. Unemployment — near full employment, around 4–5%, allowing for frictional unemployment: maximises output and reduces poverty. Inflation — the 2% CPI target: certainty for consumers and firms, protects savings, supports competitiveness.

The current account aim is a sustainable position — only a small surplus or deficit.

cards.front: Why can the macroeconomic objectives conflict, at least in the short run?
cards.back:
Policies that improve one objective often worsen another: stimulating growth and employment raises demand-pull inflation and pulls in imports; squeezing inflation with higher interest rates slows growth and costs jobs.

Governments therefore prioritise, and the priority shifts with circumstances — jobs and demand after 2008, inflation in 2022–23. AQA flags exactly this: the importance attached to objectives changes over time.

cards.front: Distinguish nominal GDP, real GDP and real GDP per capita.
cards.back:
Nominal GDP values output at current prices; real GDP adjusts for inflation, valuing output at constant prices — approximately, % change in real GDP = % change in nominal GDP − inflation.

Real GDP per capita divides real GDP by the population: average output per person, the better starting point for living standards.

cards.front: How does the RPI differ from the CPI?
cards.back:
Both track the average change in prices of a basket of goods and services and are used to calculate the inflation rate. The RPI additionally includes housing costs — mortgage interest payments and council tax — which the CPI leaves out.

RPI therefore usually runs higher than CPI, and the CPI is the measure targeted by the Bank of England.

cards.front: State the formulas for the unemployment rate and the employment rate.
cards.back:
The unemployment rate is the percentage of the labour force unemployed and actively seeking work. The employment rate is the percentage of the working-age population in work.

The denominators differ — someone economically inactive is in neither numerator, so the two rates can move independently.
cards.formulaHtml: Unemploymentrate=Unemployed/Labourforce×100Unemployment rate = Unemployed / Labour force × 100Unemploymentrate=Unemployed/Labourforce×100

cards.front: Define the current account of the balance of payments, and name the remaining spec indicator.
cards.back:
The balance of payments records all transactions between a country and the rest of the world; the current account is the part that records trade in goods and services, income flows, and current transfers.

The final indicator on the AQA list is productivity — output per worker (or per hour worked) — which drives long-run growth and competitiveness.

cards.front: Define an index number and the base year.
cards.back:
An index number expresses the value of a variable relative to a chosen base value, which is set equal to 100. The base year is the reference year all others are compared against.

Index numbers turn awkward raw figures — thousands of prices, GDP in billions — into one easy series, and they track not just prices but real GDP, wages, productivity and share prices such as the FTSE 100.

cards.front: State the index number formula, and interpret an index of 115.
cards.back: An index of 115 means the variable is 15% higher than in the base year; an index of 92 means 8% lower. The percentage change reads straight off the index only against the base year — comparing 115 with 105 is a rise of 115 ÷ 105, about 9.5%, not 10 points.

cards.front: Why does the CPI use weights, and what do the 'average family' and the 'basket' mean?
cards.back:
The CPI prices a basket of goods and services chosen to represent the spending of the average family. Each category gets a weight reflecting its share of household spending, so a 10% rise in a heavily-weighted item (housing) moves the index far more than the same rise in a lightly-weighted one (tea bags).

The weighted index is the sum of weight × price index across categories, divided by the total weight.

cards.front: A simplified basket has three categories with weights out of 1,000: housing 400 (price index 108), transport 350 (index 104), food 250 (index 112). Calculate the weighted CPI and interpret it.
cards.back:
Weight × index: housing 400 × 108 = 43,200; transport 350 × 104 = 36,400; food 250 × 112 = 28,000.

Total = 107,600; divide by total weight: 107,600 ÷ 1,000 = 107.6

Prices across the basket average 7.6% above the base year. Food rose fastest (12%), but the heavily-weighted housing category matters more to the overall index — that is what weighting does.

cards.front: Define national income, and state the national income identity.
cards.back:
National income is the total value of all goods and services produced in an economy over a given period. It can be measured in three equivalent ways — as total output, total income, or total expenditure — because one person's spending is another person's income, and all income is ultimately earned by producing output.

Hence the identity: national output ≡ national income ≡ national expenditure.

cards.front: Distinguish GDP from GNI.
cards.back:
GDP measures the value of everything produced within a country's borders, regardless of who owns the factors of production.

GNI (also called GNP) is GDP plus net income from abroad — income earned by residents from overseas assets, minus income earned by foreign residents from domestic assets. For countries with large overseas holdings or heavy inward investment, the two diverge noticeably.

cards.front: Evaluate the limitations of national income data for comparing living standards.
cards.back:
Even real GDP per capita hides much: income distribution (an average conceals inequality); the informal economy (subsistence farming, unpaid care, the hidden economy go unrecorded — a big understatement in developing countries); quality of life (health, leisure, freedom); negative externalities (polluting output still counts); the composition of output (defence spending raises GDP without raising welfare); and data reliability across countries.

The fullest single comparison is real GDP per capita at PPP; broader indices such as the HDI add health and education.

cards.front: What is purchasing power parity, and why does it matter for international comparisons?
cards.back:
PPP is an exchange rate that equalises the price of an identical basket of goods and services between two countries — what a currency actually buys at home, not what it trades for on foreign exchange markets.

Market rates mislead because they are driven by currency demand and supply, and because non-traded goods — housing, haircuts, restaurant meals — tend to be cheaper in lower-income countries. Comparing incomes at market rates therefore understates living standards in poorer economies.

cards.front: Distinguish nominal from real income, and explain what real national income indicates.
cards.back:
Nominal income is measured at current prices; real income strips out inflation, so it reflects what income can actually buy.

Rising real national income is the key indicator of economic performance: it means the economy is genuinely producing more, not just charging higher prices for the same output.

cards.front: Draw the circular flow of income for a simple two-agent economy.
cards.back:
Households and firms are linked by two pairs of flows. Real flows: households provide the factors of production — land, labour, capital, enterprise — and firms provide goods and services.

Money flows: firms pay income — rent, wages, interest, profit — and households return it as consumer expenditure, which becomes firms' revenue. The same flow measured at any point gives income = output = expenditure.
cards.svgAlt: Circular flow between firms and households: factors of production and expenditure flow to firms, goods and services and income flow to households

cards.front: Distinguish injections from withdrawals, and state the equilibrium condition.
cards.back:
Injections — investment, government spending, exports — add new spending to the circular flow; withdrawals — savings, taxation, imports — leak income out of it. National income is in equilibrium when injections equal withdrawals; if injections exceed withdrawals the flow expands, and if withdrawals exceed injections it contracts.

Full employment income is the level of national income at which all resources are fully employed — equilibrium need not occur there.

cards.front: Define aggregate demand, and give the relative importance of its components.
cards.back:
Aggregate demand is the total demand for all goods and services in an economy at a given average price level and in a given time period: AD = C + I + G + (X − M).

Consumption is the largest component at around 60% of AD; government spending around 25%; investment around 14% — the most volatile; net exports are small and often negative for the UK.

cards.front: What causes a movement along the AD curve?
cards.back:
Only a change in the average price level: a fall from PL1 to PL2 moves the economy along the curve from A to B, raising real GDP demanded from Y1 to Y2 — the inverse relationship the downward slope shows.

Any change in a determinant of AD other than the price level shifts the whole curve instead.
cards.svgAlt: Downward-sloping AD curve with a movement from point A at price level PL1 and output Y1 to point B at PL2 and Y2

cards.front: Show a shift of the AD curve, and name what causes one.
cards.back:
A change in any determinant of AD other than the price level — consumer or business confidence, interest rates, government policy, incomes abroad — changes total planned spending at every price level, shifting the curve (AD1 to AD2 for an increase, back for a decrease).

At the unchanged price level PL, real GDP demanded rises from Y1 to Y2.
cards.svgAlt: Aggregate demand curve shifting right from AD1 to AD2, raising real GDP from Y1 to Y2 at price level PL

cards.front: Use an AD/AS diagram to show macroeconomic equilibrium below full employment.
cards.back:
Short-run equilibrium is where AD crosses SRAS — here at output Y1 and price level PL1. With the LRAS curve at Yfe to the right, this equilibrium leaves a negative output gap: the economy is in balance, but below its full-employment output.

This is the AQA-required use of AD/AS analysis: reading off output and the price level, then judging the position against LRAS.
cards.svgAlt: AD and SRAS intersecting at output Y1 and price level PL1, left of the vertical LRAS curve at Yfe

cards.front: How do demand-side and supply-side shocks affect the macroeconomy?
cards.back:
A demand-side shock — a financial crisis collapsing confidence, a slump in export markets — shifts AD suddenly: output and the price level move in the same direction.

A supply-side shock — an oil price spike, a pandemic disrupting production — shifts SRAS: output and the price level move in opposite directions, the harder case for policy. Global events reach the domestic economy through both routes.

cards.front: What determines consumption, and how are MPC and MPS related?
cards.back:
Consumption — household spending on goods and services, the largest component of AD — is determined primarily by disposable income: income after direct taxes plus transfer payments.

Extra disposable income splits between spending and saving: the MPC is the proportion spent, the MPS the proportion saved, so MPC + MPS = 1. Spend £80 of an extra £100 and your MPC is 0.8.

cards.front: Beyond income, what influences consumption and saving?
cards.back:
Interest rates — higher rates raise the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving, cutting consumption and raising saving. Confidence — optimism about future income increases spending and borrowing; pessimism increases precautionary saving. Wealth effects — rising house or share prices make households spend more; falling wealth does the reverse.

The determinants of saving are the mirror image of the determinants of consumption — the same forces push the two shares in opposite directions.

cards.front: Distinguish gross from net investment, and saving from investment.
cards.back:
Investment is spending by firms on capital goods. Depreciation is the loss of value of capital goods over time due to wear and tear or obsolescence — so net investment = gross investment − depreciation: only net investment expands the capital stock.

In economics saving is not investment: saving is household income not spent; investment is firms' spending on capital. The financial sector channels one into the other.

cards.front: Explain the accelerator effect.
cards.back:
The accelerator effect is the idea that a rise in the rate of economic growth results in a larger percentage rise in investment: firms invest in new capital to meet higher expected demand, and that investment further boosts AD and growth.

It works in reverse too — a slowdown in growth produces a larger percentage fall in investment, which is part of why investment is the most volatile component of AD. AQA does not require accelerator calculations.

cards.front: Define the multiplier, and state the multiplier ratio.
cards.back:
The multiplier is the process by which an initial injection, such as an increase in government spending, investment, or exports, leads to a larger final increase in national income and real GDP: the injection becomes income, a proportion is spent (per the MPC), becomes further income, and so on.

The ratio: k = final change in real GDP ÷ initial injection — a £2bn injection producing a £6bn rise in GDP means k = 3.

cards.front: How does AQA require you to calculate the multiplier, and why does the MPC set its size?
cards.back:
From the MPC only: if MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4. (AQA states that calculations from the marginal propensities to withdraw will not be expected — that is Edexcel territory.)

The MPC governs the magnitude because it fixes how much of each round of income is re-spent: a higher MPC means less leaks away each round, so the rounds shrink more slowly and the total effect is larger.
cards.formulaHtml: M=1/(1−MPC)M = 1/(1 - MPC)M=1/(1−MPC)

cards.front: Show the multiplier effect on an AD/AS diagram.
cards.back:
The initial injection shifts AD from AD1 to AD2; the induced rounds of consumer spending carry it further to AD3. Real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2 and then Y3 — a total rise larger than the initial injection alone would give.

As the economy climbs towards capacity, more of each shift feeds the price level (PL1 to PL3) and less feeds output — the multiplier is most powerful with spare capacity.
cards.svgAlt: AD shifting right from AD1 to AD2 and then AD3 along a Keynesian LRAS1 curve, raising real GDP from Y1 to Y2 to Y3 and the price level from PL1 to PL3

cards.front: Define SRAS, and name the cost changes AQA says shift it.
cards.back:
Short-run aggregate supply is the total planned output of goods and services in an economy at a given price level, assuming that at least one factor of production, such as capital or technology, is fixed. It slopes upward because higher output brings rising unit costs, so firms need higher prices.

AQA's named shift factors: money wage rates, raw material prices, business taxation and productivity — anything changing production costs across the economy.

cards.front: Show the effect of a fall in production costs on SRAS.
cards.back:
SRAS shifts right (SRAS1 to SRAS2): firms supply more at every given price level, so at the unchanged price level PL output rises from Y1 to Y2.

Causes on the AQA list: lower money wage rates, cheaper raw materials, lighter business taxation, higher productivity. Rising costs shift the curve left instead — the anatomy of a supply-side shock.
cards.svgAlt: SRAS1 shifting right to SRAS2, raising real GDP supplied from Y1 to Y2 at the unchanged price level PL

cards.front: Define LRAS, and what the position of the vertical curve represents.
cards.back:
Long-run aggregate supply is the total potential output of an economy when all factors of production are fully and efficiently employed — the economy's productive capacity.

The position of the vertical LRAS curve represents the normal capacity level of output; shifts in LRAS are long-run growth or decline, equivalent to the PPF moving.

cards.front: Name AQA's fundamental determinants of LRAS.
cards.back:
Technology, productivity, attitudes, enterprise, factor mobility and economic incentives — the AQA list is broader than a factors-of-production checklist, reaching into how willing and able an economy is to use what it has.

AQA also stresses the institutional structure of the economy — notably a banking system that channels funds into business investment — as a determinant of aggregate supply.

cards.front: Draw and explain the Keynesian AS curve.
cards.back:
The curve AQA names explicitly: L-shaped, with three phases — perfectly elastic at low output, where spare capacity lets firms expand without raising prices; upward sloping as resources grow scarce; vertical at full capacity Yfe, where extra demand only raises prices.

It embodies the Keynesian belief that the economy can sit below full employment for a long time.
cards.svgAlt: L-shaped Keynesian LRAS curve: flat at low output, sloping upward as capacity nears, vertical at full-capacity output Yfe

cards.front: Show underlying economic growth on an AD/AS diagram.
cards.back:
Underlying (long-run) growth is a rightward shift of the LRAS curve, from LRAS1 to LRAS2: normal capacity output rises from Yfe1 to Yfe2.

It is driven by the fundamental determinants — technology, productivity, enterprise, factor mobility, incentives — improving the quantity or quality of what the economy can produce.
cards.svgAlt: Vertical LRAS1 curve shifting right to LRAS2, raising full-employment output from Yfe1 to Yfe2
